population_description: Adults aged 18 years or older who had received a COVID-19 vaccine, with and without pre-existing COVID-19-related chemosensory impairment; most participants aged 25-64 years (71.6%)
taste_types_reported: dysgeusia (reported as distorted taste, single category); unspecified taste dysfunction (general taste impairment/loss)
taste_measurement: other-as-stated: self-reported change in taste (improved / no change / worsened) after each vaccine dose
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Pre-vaccination distorted taste reported by 380 participants; 416 reported impairments in both smell and taste (of 599 of 1220 participants with complete taste and smell data, 49%, reporting pre-vaccination COVID-19 chemosensory impairment)
onset_timing: For post-vaccination chemosensory changes: among 75 participants who reported timing and duration, approximately two-thirds indicated onset on the day following vaccination and most reported duration longer than 1 month
recovery_any_as_printed: Post-vaccination improvement (not labelled complete recovery): distorted taste improved in 12%-21% of participants with pre-existing distorted taste depending on vaccine dose; improvement in general smell or taste in 3%-8% of participants with pre-existing impairment depending on dose; 94% or more of all participants reported no change in general smell or taste
pathogenesis_finding: The biological mechanisms underlying post-vaccination changes in chemosensory function remain uncertain; transient inflammatory responses within the olfactory neuroepithelium or immune-mediated effects related to residual viral material following SARS-CoV-2 infection were proposed, and the authors state these mechanisms remain speculative
special_populations_notes: Participants pregnant after the outbreak of COVID (n = 69), younger than 18 years (n = 33), and with pre-existing health conditions (n = 228) were excluded
funding_conflicts: Funding not reported; Acknowledgments: Liang-Dar Hwang is supported by an Australian Research Council Early Discovery Researcher Award (DE240100014). Conflicts: Kathrin Ohla works at dsm-firmenich, the company had no influence on study design or interpretation; the other authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Vaccination was the exposure, not a treatment started for taste dysfunction, so Q3 fields left blank. Vaccine side effects as printed (not Q3 adverse events): fatigue 34.6% after first dose, headache 32.6%, fever 32.0%, muscle pain 29.0%, chills 25.2%, joint pain 22.1%. Quote: 'The survey assessed distorted taste as a single category and did not distinguish between specific qualitative gustatory disorders.' Quote: 'More than 90% of participants reported no change in general smell or taste following vaccination, regardless of pre-existing chemosensory impairment.'

population_description: COVID-19-positive patients over five years of age followed by the San Miguelito Health Region, Panama, from July 7, 2021 through November 2, 2022; unvaccinated patients or patients whose recorded doses were exclusively Pfizer-BioNTech
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (self-reported ageusia during telephone follow-up call)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Ageusia was reported by 507 patients (9.48%); by dose category: 192 (17.50%) with zero doses, 99 (27.35%) with one dose, 171 (9.90%) with two doses, 45 (2.08%) with three to four doses
special_populations_notes: Children included (age group 6-17 years: 556 (10.40%)); adults aged 63 years or older included; chronic conditions counted included diabetes 464 (8.68%), chronic kidney disease 14 (0.26%) and immunosuppression 17 (0.32%)
funding_conflicts: All authors declared no financial support was received from any organization for the submitted work and no financial or other relationships that might have an interest in the submitted work
extractor_notes: Virus confirmation: patients are described as COVID-19-positive with swab dates recorded, but the test/assay type is not stated in the paper. Vaccine dose category is an exposure, not a treatment for taste dysfunction, so Q3 fields left blank. Quote: aORs for ageusia vs two doses were 1.87 (95% CI 1.48-2.38) for zero doses, 2.68 (95% CI 1.99-3.60) for one dose and 0.26 (95% CI 0.18-0.36) for three to four doses in primary adjusted models; after adjustment for swab month none remained statistically significant. No taste pathogenesis mechanism is proposed or tested; an ACE2-neutralization association from a cited study is described as biological context without establishing a dose effect, so Q2 fields left blank.

country_setting: Brazil (single centre: Interdisciplinary Laboratory for Health Promotion Intervention (LIIPS), Unicesumar, Maringa, Parana)
population_description: Post-COVID-19 individuals aged 19-65 years who had contracted COVID-19 between March 1 and July 1, 2021, identified through referrals from the municipal hospital of Maringa following hospital discharge; all had received the first dose of a COVID-19 vaccine
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (standardized questionnaire, dichotomous yes/no self-report; no objective olfactory or gustatory testing was performed)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Ageusia (n = 121); No ageusia (n = 80), of 201 participants (Table 2); no overall percentage for ageusia printed
pathogenesis_finding: Ageusia was independently associated with memory deficit (adjusted OR = 2.91; 95% CI 1.47-5.75) and aural fullness (adjusted OR = 4.08; 95% CI 1.02-16.30) but VO2peak did not differ by ageusia (mean difference 1.36 mL/kg/min; p = 0.244); discussion interprets anosmia/ageusia as reflecting a central neuroinflammatory phenotype, citing cytokine overproduction and ACE2-mediated neuronal damage from prior literature
special_populations_notes: Diabetes Mellitus in 32 (15.9%) of the sample; debilitating neurological diseases or mobility limitations requiring a cane or wheelchair were exclusion criteria; age restricted to 19-65 years
funding_conflicts: Article Processing Charge funded by Coordenacao de Aperfeicoamento de Pessoal de Nivel Superior - Brasil (CAPES); study supported by Cesumar University (UniCesumar), Cesumar Institute of Science, Technology and Innovation (ICETI), Araucaria Foundation PPSUS and CNPq, and a research productivity grant for the last author (Araucaria Foundation); authors declare no competing interests
extractor_notes: Single assessment at mean infection-evaluation time 214.5 +/- 116.4 days after acute infection. Duration of ageusia as printed in Table 3 (among n = 121 with ageusia): < 2 months (n = 93), 2-4 months (n = 11), 4-6 months (n = 5), > 6 months (n = 12); the paper does not label a persistent-at->=12-weeks proportion, so persistent field left as not reported. Confirmation quote: 'confirmed diagnosis of COVID-19 through a qualitative molecular test (RT-PCR)'.

design: other-as-stated: genome-wide machine learning analysis of two COVID-19 cohorts
country_setting: United States of America (University of Iowa, Iowa City; NIH All of Us Research Program)
N_total: UI cohort N = 187; AoU cohort N = 947 (no combined total printed)
population_description: Patients with COVID-19 in the University of Iowa whole genome sequencing cohort (recruited 30 June 2020 to 31 July 2022; patients under four years of age excluded; no documented history of olfactory or gustatory dysfunction prior to COVID-19) and the All of Us Research Program COVID-19 cohort
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (symptoms collected through surveys or electronic medical records; binary phenotype derived from yes/no survey responses)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: UI cohort: 95 cases and 92 controls for the loss of taste phenotype (of 187), comprising 8 reporting only a loss of taste and 87 reporting a loss in smell and taste; AoU cohort: taste reported only combined with smell as loss of smell or taste, 421 cases and 526 controls (of 947)
pathogenesis_finding: Analysis prioritized several novel and known candidate host genetic factors involved in immune response, neuronal signaling, and calcium signaling supporting previously proposed hypotheses for anosmia/ageusia in COVID-19; highest held-out test set AUROC was 0.735 for variant analysis and 0.798 for gene analysis in the UI cohort and 0.687 for variant analysis in the AoU cohort
special_populations_notes: Children: patients under four years of age at consent excluded from the UI cohort; minors participated with parent/guardian consent (saliva collection kits for minors described)
funding_conflicts: Funded by the University of Iowa Interdisciplinary Genetics T32 Predoctoral Training Grant T32 GM 008629, the Integrated DNA Technologies Bioinformatics Fellowship Program, and University of Iowa Stead Family Department of Pediatrics departmental and start-up funds; funders had no role in the study; authors declared no competing interests exist
extractor_notes: T11 = host genetic susceptibility (other). Introduction as printed: 'The most probable cause of the loss of taste with COVID-19 is the viral invasion of gustatory nerves, taste receptor cells, and the olfactory epithelium' and pro-inflammatory cytokines are proposed as contributing factors. Confirmation quote (UI cohort): patients reported 'a positive SARS-CoV-2 infection with antibody or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing ... or presumed positive by being symptomatic and in a household with someone who tested positive', hence mixed. No intervention was administered, so Q3 fields left blank despite the record's Q3 tag. AoU taste cannot be separated from smell.

population_description: Individuals aged 18 years or older with sudden chemosensory dysfunction during the COVID-19 pandemic after 27 February 2020 (date of the first confirmed Danish case), completing a questionnaire four years after symptom onset; median age at enrolment 46 years (range: 18-87)
taste_measurement: patient-reported scale named (questionnaire using validated self-report items; self-reported CD recovery; WHO-5 instrument for mental well-being; no psychophysical measurement)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported (cohort was defined by sudden chemosensory dysfunction; the GD-specific number is in Table 2 / supplementary material and is not printed in the main text; text states most participants reported combined OD and GD)
onset_timing: not reported (sudden CD after 27 February 2020 was an eligibility criterion; mean time from symptom onset to the baseline questionnaire was 82 days (IQR: 28-103))
recovery_complete_as_printed: Full GD recovery at four years: 59% of male participants achieved full GD recovery compared with 51% of females (p = 0.028); overall, 43% reported full recovery from CD and 152 (43%) reported full subjective recovery (CD composite)
recovery_any_as_printed: not reported (partial recovery was grouped with no improvement as the Persistent CD group; no taste-specific any-recovery proportion printed)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: not reported for taste alone (persistent CD at four years, defined as partial recovery or no improvement, was highest in the 45-59 years group at 68.3%, vs 52.4% at 30-44 years, 49.1% at 60 years or older and 45.3% at 18-29 years; CD composite)
pathogenesis_finding: No mechanism was tested; as a measurement caveat the authors state reported taste loss may reflect impaired flavour perception rather than true GD, because the study relied entirely on self-reported data with no psychophysical measurement of olfactory or gustatory function
follow_up_duration: Four years after symptom onset (mean follow-up was 1,496 days (IQR: 1,398-1,616))
funding_conflicts: Funding: None. Conflicts: AWF reports financial support from or interest in Region Midtjyllands Sundhedsvidenskabelige Forskningsfond, Folkeuniversitetet; all authors submitted ICMJE disclosure forms
extractor_notes: TASTE-SEPARATE resolution: GD (taste) recovery is reported separately from OD by sex (59% vs 51% full GD recovery), but the taste-specific prevalence denominator is not printed in the main text. Confirmation: 'Although most participants had test-verified COVID-19, lack of testing was not an exclusion criterion'; PCR-confirmed participants (n = 221; full recovery 36.7%) were compared with those with no positive PCR (n = 135; 52.6%); limitations state PCR-confirmed COVID-19 was 62% vs 38% without. Treatments (vaccination, olfactory training, steroids) are discussed from other studies only, so Q3 fields left blank.

population_description: Individuals who had recovered from SARS-CoV-2, recruited from the community and enrolled at 3, 6 or 12 months after viral-clearance; age 59.9 +/- 8.6 years (84 females and 36 males); confirmed neurodegenerative diseases and blood-borne diseases excluded; all reported being symptom-free at enrolment
taste_types_reported: hypogeusia (ODOFIN score < 9; analysis groups were normogeusia vs hypogeusia/ageusia)
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (ODOFIN Taste Strips 50; total score 0-16 across sweet, sour, salty and bitter)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Hypogeusia at Visit 1: 27 (22.5%) of 120 (Group 1, 3 months: 10 (25.0%); Group 2, 6 months: 12 (30.0%); Group 3, 12 months: 5 (12.5%)); at Visit 2: 18 (15.0%) of 120
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Hypogeusia in Group 3 (enrolled 12 months after viral-clearance): 5 (12.5%) at Visit 1 and 5 (12.5%) at Visit 2, three months later
taste_score_change_as_printed: Gustatory function score (mean +/- SD), total cohort: Visit 1 10.77 +/- 2.73; Visit 2 11.18 +/- 2.40; two-way ANOVA revealed no significant main effect of recovery group or within-group differences on ODOFIN scores; abstract states gustatory function had largely normalised at the first visit across all groups and remained stable at follow-up
pathogenesis_finding: No significant correlations were observed between alpha-synuclein and gustatory function at either visit (rho = 0.061, p = 0.533 at Visit 1; rho = 0.067, p = 0.494 at Visit 2) and no other biomarker (Abeta42, GFAP, S100B, NSE, ferritin) correlated significantly with gustatory function; alpha-synuclein correlated with olfactory performance at Visit 1 only (rho = -0.258, p = 0.007)
special_populations_notes: Older adults: mean age 59.9 +/- 8.6 years; confirmed diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases and blood-borne diseases were exclusion criteria
follow_up_duration: Enrolled at 3, 6 or 12 months after viral-clearance (Visit 1) and re-evaluated three months later (Visit 2)
funding_conflicts: Funded by the Health and Medical Research Fund (HMRF) - Commissioned Research on COVID-19 from the Health Bureau of Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (reference COVID1903007) and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (reference P0052607-ZZUA); authors declare no competing interests
extractor_notes: T11 = protein aggregation-related processes / alpha-synuclein susceptibility as framed by the authors. Introduction as printed: gustatory dysfunction 'may arise from viral replication within taste receptor cells, evidenced by SARS-CoV-2 co-localisation with type II taste cell markers and the ACE2 receptor within taste buds' (T1), with inflammatory responses also proposed (T5). Confirmation: recovered status confirmed by 'conversion from positive to negative rapid antigen (lateral flow) test or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test'. Recovery proportions for taste are not printed as recovery rates (only hypogeusia counts at each visit), so recovery fields left as not reported rather than computed.

N_total: 42 (long COVID cohort assessed for taste); single-cell RNA sequencing in 6 LC-D individuals and 6 healthy controls
population_description: Individuals with long COVID and self-reported taste loss lasting longer than 60 days after a SARS-CoV-2-positive laboratory (RT-PCR) test, recruited through the Indiana University School of Medicine COVID-19 Research Registry; LC cohort average age 51.7 +/- 14 years, male-to-female ratio 13:28; healthy controls were cryopreserved pre-COVID saliva samples
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (Waterless Empirical Taste Test (WETT); scores for each of five tastes range 0-8; subjects with WETT scores < 2 were considered dysgeusic)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: In the LC cohort (n = 42): impaired bitter taste 30% (13/42), impaired sweet 29% (12/42), impaired sour 17% (7/42), impaired salty 19% (8/42); complete ageusia was observed in 5%, and phantom or faulty taste (perceived in response to blank strips) in 11.9%
onset_timing: not reported (eligibility required taste loss lasting longer than 60 days)
pathogenesis_finding: Salivary epithelial cell transcriptomes from individuals with bitter taste dysfunction (LC-D) showed downregulation of specific Type II and III taste receptor genes critical for bitter taste perception, genes involved in cytoskeletal dynamics and taste cell-nerve synapse assembly, and microbial defense markers TLR2 and TLR4 suggesting chronic inflammation, supporting a model of sustained dysregulated epithelial turnover in LC-D (8472 cells sequenced; 7321 cells post-QC)
funding_conflicts: Funded by support from Delta Dental Research Program to MS, grant number #44-762-54; authors declare no conflicts of interest and funders had no role in the study
extractor_notes: Design is a human mechanistic single-cell transcriptomic study of salivary epithelial cells (SECs), not a prevalence cohort: the 42-person LC cohort provides the taste-test percentages and 12 samples (6 LC-D with bitter taste scores <= 1, 6 healthy controls) provide the scRNA-seq data. No intervention was administered, so Q3 fields left blank.

N_total: 96 (100 individuals enrolled; 4 samples excluded due to low genotyping quality)
population_description: Unrelated, nonclinical healthy volunteers aged over 18 years with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection in the past year during 2020-2022 and no chronic diseases; analysed groups were OGD (olfactory/gustatory dysfunction) n = 48 and no-OGD n = 48
taste_types_reported: dysgeusia (self-reported taste dysfunction; discussion also terms loss of taste ageusia)
taste_measurement: patient-reported scale named (38-question survey adapted based on MCSTQ-Sc; presence of self-reported taste dysfunction)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Taste-specific prevalence not printed in the text (study groups were defined by combined olfactory and gustatory dysfunction: OGD n = 48 and no-OGD n = 48 of 96; specific loss patterns are shown only in Figure 2); Discussion states for ageusia (loss of taste): 'The 15% incidence observed here'
pathogenesis_finding: Statistically significant differences were observed for HCN4 variants c.*2393C > G (p = 0.013) and c.2556G > A (p = 0.026), PLCB2 variants c.3037-55T > C (p = 0.019) and c.582+958_582+959inv (p = 0.021), and TAS1R1 variant c.1594+41G > A (p = 0.03), which indicate possible association to taste dysfunction in response to virus infection; all had Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p = 0.030
special_populations_notes: Adults over 18 years only (age under 18 years was an exclusion criterion); presence of chronic diseases was an exclusion criterion
funding_conflicts: Supported by a grant of the Ministry of Science, Higher Education and Youth of Sarajevo Canton (contract no.: 27-02-11-41250-40/21); authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: T11 = host genetic susceptibility to taste changes (other). T1/T5 are explicitly proposed in the introduction/discussion (ACE2 receptors within taste buds; cytokine storm inducing secondary damage to gustatory function); the study's own new evidence is genetic. Confirmation quote: inclusion required 'confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection in the past year by a primary care physician after the PCR test'. Because grouping is by combined OGD, taste-only case numbers cannot be extracted from the text; do not use the 48/96 split as a taste prevalence.

N_total: 2340 (complete responses; 3028 submitted the survey and 3347 were recruited)
population_description: Non-institutionalised adults aged 18 years or older residing in Austria (n = 1,023), Germany (n = 1,031) and Switzerland (n = 286), general population online survey conducted in January 2025
taste_types_reported: unspecified taste dysfunction (taste impairment / taste loss)
taste_measurement: patient-reported scale named (Smell-Qx questionnaire, a validated patient-reported outcome measure with 70 items including a gustation domain)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Taste Impairment: Yes 442 (18.9%) of 2340; No 1898 (81.1%); by country: Austria 168 (16.4%), Germany 197 (19.1%), Switzerland 77 (26.9%)
recovery_complete_as_printed: not reported (improvement since onset was reported, not complete recovery)
recovery_any_as_printed: Taste (Table 3, n = 423 with taste recovery data): Improved 193 (45.6%), No Change 152 (35.9%), Worsened 78 (18.4%); text states 54.3% (n = 230) reported no improvement or worsening of 'taste' loss, equal to 9.8% (n = 230) of the total sample (N = 2,340)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: not reported (no onset dates or >=12-week time point; symptoms unchanged or worsening since onset were reported for 62% or fewer across SATDs, with taste no-change/worsening 54.3% of the taste subgroup)
funding_conflicts: Funding was received via the Rosetrees Trust; the authors have no conflicts of interest to declare
extractor_notes: Virus is not a confirmed cohort exposure: this is a general-population survey of smell and taste disorders of mixed aetiology. Of respondents with SATDs who provided a suspected aetiology (454 (48.0%)), all (100%) indicated symptoms began following an acute upper respiratory tract infection such as a cold, influenza, or COVID-19, by self-report with no laboratory confirmation. Table 2 taste total (442) differs from Table 3 taste total (423) because 19 participants did not respond to the recovery item (footnote as printed). No intervention was administered in this study (treatments are discussed from the literature only), so Q3 fields left blank despite the record's Q3 tag; no pathogenesis mechanism is proposed with evidence, so Q2 fields left blank.

N_total: 104 (from an original pool of 201 adults with laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection)
population_description: Adults with polymerase chain reaction-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection during the first and second pandemic waves, assessed approximately 75 days after diagnosis; median age 58.5 years (IQR: 16.2); 69 men (66.3%) and 35 women (33.7%)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (olfactory dysfunction and dysgeusia recorded as dichotomous present/absent variables)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Dysgeusia was reported by 36.5% (n = 38) of 104 participants; alterations in taste perception were absent in 63.5% (n = 66)
onset_timing: not reported (the paper states detailed information regarding symptom onset, duration, or progression during the acute phase was not collected)
pathogenesis_finding: No statistically significant associations were observed between baseline expression levels of ACE2, TMPRSS2, furin, or NRP1 and the presence of olfactory dysfunction or dysgeusia in either adjusted continuous or categorical models; the authors conclude dysgeusia does not appear to be directly determined by isolated baseline expression of SARS-CoV-2 entry receptors and support a multifactorial model involving temporal receptor regulation, inflammatory processes, and host-related factors
funding_conflicts: This research received no external funding; the authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Single post-acute assessment approximately 75 days after confirmed diagnosis, at which participants were asked whether they had experienced gustatory dysfunction at any time during their COVID-19 illness; hence follow-up duration recorded as not reported. T1 = viral-entry receptor expression hypothesis tested directly in nasal/pharyngeal samples; introduction also postulates inflammatory (T5) and neuronal / olfactory nerve and central (T3) mechanisms. No intervention was administered, so Q3 fields left blank.

N_total: 52 analysed (26 patients with dysosmia/dysgeusia, Group A; 26 without these symptoms, Group B; 95 met inclusion and exclusion criteria among 520 patients admitted with COVID-19)
population_description: Patients admitted with acute COVID-19 to Kanagawa Cancer Center between September 13, 2021 and September 30, 2023; Group B was matched on age, disease severity and cancer; adolescents aged <20 years, pregnant women and people with pre-existing taste or smell impairment were excluded
taste_types_reported: dysgeusia; ageusia; hypogeusia; hypergeusia / hypersensitivity to salty, bitter or sour taste (as listed per patient in Table 1)
taste_measurement: other-as-stated: chief complaint at admission, confirmed by the attending physician for COVID-19 (present/absent; no validated gustatory test)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Not estimable as a prevalence from this case-control sample as printed; abstract states dysgeusia exhibited heterogeneous manifestations, primarily ageusia or hypogeusia, followed by hypersensitivity to salty taste; Table 3 (N = 50 with known vaccination status): Dysgeusia Positive 6 unvaccinated and 15 vaccinated; Dysgeusia Negative 5 unvaccinated and 24 vaccinated
onset_timing: Dysosmia/dysgeusia were chief complaints at admission during acute COVID-19; average timepoint of blood sampling after COVID-19 onset was 4.69 +/- 2.51 days in Group A vs 3.62 +/- 2.22 days in Group B
pathogenesis_finding: Group A showed significantly lower Trp levels [median 9.70 ug/mL (range 4.59-13.89) vs 10.40 (7.52-13.34), p = 0.031] and higher Kyn-Trp ratio [61.34 (40.47-384.2) vs 53.52 (26.13-86.64), p < 0.037] and quinolinic acid (QUIN) levels [574.39 nM (100.39-11909) vs 443.65 (83.09-998.3), p < 0.0169]; authors conclude serum KTR and QUIN may serve as biomarkers for dysgeusia/dysosmia during acute COVID-19 and targeting the kynurenine pathway is a promising strategy
special_populations_notes: Pregnant women excluded; adolescents aged <20 years excluded; pre-existing taste or smell impairment excluded; current smokers excluded; hospital is a cancer centre and controls were matched for cancer (patients with cancer included)
funding_conflicts: Supported by the Kanagawa Prefecture Hospital Cancer Fund [grant number 2022CancerC358], funder had no role in the study; Jun Tsukiji reports receiving a scholarship from Shionogi Pharma (the Kanagawa Prefecture Hospital Cancer Fund [grant number 2022CancerC358]); the other authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: T11 = kynurenine-pathway / quinolinic acid neuroimmune modulation (other); IDO/TDO activity is inflammation-linked, hence T5 also mapped. Confirmation: 'SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected using a nucleic acid test or antigen quantitative test from nasopharyngeal or pharyngeal swab samples obtained upon admission.' Caution: Group A is the composite dysosmia and/or dysgeusia group, so the biomarker comparisons are for the composite, not dysgeusia alone. No treatment for taste dysfunction was administered or compared (COVID-19 treatments were recorded as clinical data only; kynurenine-pathway targeting and vaccination are discussed as future/preventive strategies), so Q3 fields left blank despite the record's Q3 tag.

design: other-as-stated: retrospective study (single-arm, no control group)
N_total: 71 (34 complaining of loss of smell and taste; 36 complaining only of smell loss; 1 complaining only of taste loss)
population_description: Long COVID patients infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the Omicron variant pandemic in Taiwan who had persistent loss of smell and/or taste for >1 month after infection between May 2022 and December 2023, with normal olfactory and gustatory functions preinfection; patients with sinonasal disease on endoscopy, recent head trauma or autoimmune diseases were excluded
taste_types_reported: hypogeusia (objectively measured on WETT); loss of taste as complained by patients
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named (Waterless Empirical Taste Test (WETT)) plus telephone self-report at follow-up
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Among 34 patients complaining of loss of smell and taste, WETT results showed gustatory dysfunction in 8 patients (23.5%) at the first visit; among 36 patients complaining only of smell loss, WETT results showed gustatory dysfunction in 6 patients (16.7%); the one patient complaining only of taste loss had a WETT score of 1 at the first visit
onset_timing: Persistent loss for >1 month after infection at enrolment; interval between SARS-CoV-2 infection and the first outpatient visit ranged from 1 to 11 months (mean + SD: 2.53 + 2.21 months) in the smell-and-taste-loss group and 1 to 7 months (mean + SD: 2.47 + 2.72 months) in the smell-loss-only group
recovery_complete_as_printed: Smell-and-taste-loss group (n = 34), telephone follow-up at a mean of 10.35 months: gustatory function was completely restored in 18 patients, partially restored in 12 patients, and without improvement in 4 patients; text states complete recovery in 52.9% of the patients (Table 1 phone review: no complete recovery in 16/34 (47.1%))
recovery_any_as_printed: Smell-and-taste-loss group (n = 34): the improvement rate for gustatory function was 88.2% at telephone follow-up (mean 10.35 months); Discussion as printed: 30 patients (88.2%) reported improved gustatory function
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: After 2-4 months of treatment, 3 of 18 retested smell-and-taste-loss patients (16.7%) remained hypogeusic on WETT; at telephone follow-up (mean 10.35 months), 16/34 (47.1%) reported no complete recovery of gustation
taste_score_change_as_printed: In the 18 retested smell-and-taste-loss patients, WETT scores ranged from 14 to 37 (mean + SD: 26.28 + 7.13) before treatment and from 10 to 39 (mean + SD: 28.61 + 8.38) after treatment, and increased significantly after treatment (p = 0.019); among the three hypogeusic patients, none showed improvement in the WETT score (Table 1 gustatory improvement rate 0/3 (0%)). Taste-loss-only patient: WETT score 1 at first visit, increased to 31 after 2 months of treatment
pathogenesis_finding: Objective testing showed most patients complaining of gustatory dysfunction did not really have a taste problem but had developed a flavor disorder associated with olfactory dysfunction (T4); hypothesised gustatory mechanisms as printed: indirect damage to taste receptors due to infected epithelial cells and the local inflammation that follows, and expression of angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 in taste organs after viral infection of the salivary gland
intervention: Oral zinc and steroids (zinc gluconate and oral prednisolone)
intervention_dose_course: Oral prednisolone (10 mg bid) and a zinc gluconate tablet (10 mg tid) were prescribed for a month; eligible patients then took another 1-3 months course of oral prednisolone and zinc gluconate (second tests after 2-4 months of treatment as printed)
N_per_arm: Single arm: 71 patients treated; retested after treatment: 18 of the 34 smell-and-taste-loss patients and 21 of the 36 smell-loss-only patients; the taste-loss-only patient (n = 1) was also retested
treatment_recovery_as_printed: Gustatory outcomes, smell-and-taste-loss group: after 2-4 months of treatment, gustatory dysfunction in 3/18 (16.7%) on retest WETT with improvement in 0/3 (0%) of hypogeusic patients; at telephone follow-up (mean + SD 10.35 + 5.50 months, range 2-19 months), gustatory improvement 30/34 (88.2%) with complete recovery in 52.9%. Taste-loss-only patient (71-year-old woman): after 2 months of treatment with prednisolone and zinc her WETT score increased from 1 to 31, and at five months after the first visit she reported partial recovery of taste function by telephone
special_populations_notes: none reported (exclusions included autoimmune diseases, recent head trauma and sinonasal disease; the single taste-loss-only patient was a 71-year-old woman)
follow_up_duration: Telephone follow-up interval from the first outpatient visit ranged from 2 to 19 months (mean + SD: 10.35 + 5.50 months) in the smell-and-taste-loss group and from 2 to 18 months (mean + SD: 10.42 + 5.35 months) in the smell-loss-only group
funding_conflicts: The author(s) received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article; the author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: No control group: authors state 'we did not include control patients who did not receive medical treatment in this study' and that about half of patients did not return for the second objective test, so treatment effects are pre-post only. Virus confirmation method (e.g. PCR) is not stated in the paper; infection is described as occurring during the Omicron prevalent period in Taiwan. Patients who reported complete recovery after the first month of treatment were excluded from the study as printed in Methods, which biases the retested sample. First-author name as printed: Yi-Fang Chiang.
